prompt: What did Renata write before any requirement in the job description?

choices.text: The salary range
choices.why: A good thing to include, but not what came first.

choices.text: A copy of the last description, trimmed
choices.why: She started again rather than editing the fourteen-requirement page.

choices.text: A list of the technologies the team uses, so candidates know what to expect on day one
choices.why: Technologies went into the not-required list, after the paragraph.

choices.text: What the person will actually do in their first six months
choices.why: Right: every requirement then had to trace back to that paragraph.

prompt: Which of these belongs in the must list for Agenda’s E2, by the lesson’s test?
hint: Could somebody without it do the work, with help?

choices.text: 5+ years of Python
choices.why: Years of a technology predict little, and Python went in the not-required list.

choices.text: Experience with time zones
choices.why: Useful, and learnable on the job; it was listed as not required.

choices.text: Has built and run a backend service in production
choices.why: Right: the job is owning one, so somebody without it could not do the work.

choices.text: A degree in computer science or a related field from a recognised university
choices.why: The lesson lists a degree, when the job does not need one, as a requirement that predicts little.

prompt: What did Gaucher, Friesen and Kay find in 2011?

choices.text: Women apply only when they meet every requirement
choices.why: That is the disputed HP figure, not this study.

choices.text: Masculine-coded wording made jobs less appealing to women, without changing how qualified they felt
choices.why: Right: the wording alone changed who would apply.

choices.text: Shorter adverts get more applications
choices.why: Not what this study measured.

choices.text: Salary ranges increase applications from everyone
choices.why: Not this study.

prompt: A requirement is in the job description and no interviewer assesses it. What does the lesson call it?

choices.text: A must
choices.why: A must is assessed; that is what makes it one.

choices.text: A filter that works before the interviews, so it does not need to be assessed again later on
choices.why: Nothing filters on a requirement nobody checks.

choices.text: Culture fit
choices.why: Culture fit is a different problem: an unstated criterion.

choices.text: Decoration
choices.why: Right: and one assessed but not in the description is a surprise to the candidate.

prompt: In Agenda’s funnel, 15 people reached the technical interview and 6 passed. What percentage passed?
Agenda’s funnel started with 240 applications and ended with 1 accepted offer. How many applications per hire is that?
Why did Caju lose one of its two offers?

choices.text: The candidate accepted elsewhere while Caju took a week to decide
choices.why: Right: a slow end to the process loses people all the earlier effort was spent on.

choices.text: The salary was too low
choices.why: The lesson gives the delay as the reason.

choices.text: She failed a reference check
choices.why: Not in the story.

choices.text: Renata changed her mind after a second look at the candidate’s technical interview notes
choices.why: Nothing like that happened.

prompt: What does the lesson say a funnel that relies on referrals ends up doing?

choices.text: Hiring faster and better, which is why Renata dropped the public advert for later roles
choices.why: She kept the advert and widened where it went.

choices.text: Breaking employment law
choices.why: Nothing illegal is suggested.

choices.text: Paying referral bonuses that cost more than recruiters
choices.why: Cost is not the point made.

choices.text: Hiring the same team again
choices.why: Right: referrals resemble the existing team, which is efficient and narrows the pool.

prompt: Which habits does the lesson give for the candidates who are not hired? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Detailed written feedback on every interview
choices.why: Not one of the habits in the lesson.

choices.text: Nobody waits more than a week between stages
choices.why: Yes: good candidates are interviewing elsewhere.

choices.text: Everybody who spoke to somebody gets an answer
choices.why: Yes: a short message within a week of each stage.

choices.text: A guaranteed interview for the next opening
choices.why: Not in the lesson.

choices.text: A call, not a message, after the final interviews
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Six candidates reached the final interviews, each met by four interviewers for 1.5 hours including the write-up. How many interviewer hours is that?
About how long was it from opening Agenda’s E2 role to Lucas’s first day?
hint: Nine weeks plus a month of notice.

choices.text: Four weeks
choices.why: That is roughly the notice period alone.

choices.text: Nine weeks
choices.why: That was to the accepted offer; the notice period came after.

choices.text: Thirteen weeks
choices.why: Right: nine to an accepted offer, then thirty days’ notice.

choices.text: Six months, counting the time for Lucas to become fully productive on the team
choices.why: Ramp-up came after his first day; the question is about the first day.

prompt: What should Renata’s plan have assumed for a new engineer, by the lesson?

choices.text: Help from the new person in the same quarter
choices.why: That was the July promise to Helena, and it did not hold.

choices.text: Nothing, since hiring is the recruiter’s job and does not touch the team’s plans
choices.why: It cost the team more than two weeks of engineering hours.

choices.text: Two weeks of onboarding, then full speed
choices.why: Lesson 18 shows ramp-up takes far longer than two weeks.

choices.text: A quarter to hire and a quarter to ramp up
choices.why: Right: by the time Lucas contributed fully, the quarter in the plan was over.

prompt: In week six, a candidate is strong in three interviews and weak in the one on a must. The team is behind. What reasoning does Renata use?

choices.text: Three of four is good enough under pressure
choices.why: The weak interview was on a must, which by definition he needs.

choices.text: An empty seat costs a month; a hire who cannot do the job costs far more, so the must list holds
choices.why: Right: the bar was written before the pressure so that a tired manager compares against a document.

choices.text: Hire him and plan an improvement plan if needed
choices.why: Hiring with a plan for failure is the cost the lesson warns about.

choices.text: Ask Helena to decide
choices.why: The offer is Renata’s decision, per lesson 2’s page.
